m5-t1.introduction: Choose a small channel mix you can operate well. Tie platform choice to customer behaviour, a content promise and a useful business outcome.

sections.title: Attention is also a team capacity problem
sections.explanation: Spreading the same time across too many accounts leaves less time to research, respond and improve.

items.label: Five accounts: time per account
items.detail: A hypothetical ten-hour weekly budget split evenly.

items.label: Two accounts: time per account
items.detail: The same weekly budget split between two priorities.

sections.takeaway: This is time allocation, not a prediction that a particular number of platforms performs best.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

sections.title: Choose the job before the platform
sections.explanation: Platform audiences and features evolve. Use the audience’s actual behaviour and the content’s job rather than stereotypes.

items.label: Discovery / demonstration
items.detail: Choose places where relevant people watch and explore.

items.label: Professional credibility
items.detail: Choose contexts where expertise and work evidence are useful.

items.label: Local conversation
items.detail: Choose a manageable route for real questions and support.

items.label: Deep explanation
items.detail: Choose a format that can answer the question properly.

sections.takeaway: Review the current platform landscape before a cohort; do not treat a platform label as a permanent strategy.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The social strategy sentence
sections.explanation: A compact strategy connects the audience, promise, format, cadence and outcome so a teammate can evaluate a new idea.

items.label: For whom?
items.detail: Name a specific audience and its situation.

items.label: What value?
items.detail: State the recurring question or benefit you will deliver.

items.label: How / how often?
items.detail: Choose a sustainable format and rhythm.

items.label: To what end?
items.detail: Define the useful action and how it will be measured.

sections.takeaway: Keep a stop-list: what you will deliberately not publish or operate this cycle.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Applause and outcomes live on different branches
sections.explanation: Likes can describe a response but do not by themselves show business value.

items.label: Reach
items.detail: Did relevant people have a chance to see the content?

items.label: Meaningful engagement
items.detail: Did saves, replies or questions indicate usefulness?

items.label: Qualified action
items.detail: Did people make an appropriate enquiry or visit?

items.label: Cost / effort
items.detail: Was the result worth the time and spend?

sections.takeaway: Define denominators and time windows before comparing engagement rates.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Why might a stop-list improve a social strategy?
checkpoint.answer: It protects capacity for the audience, formats and channels that serve the goal. A deliberate “not now” is more useful than five neglected accounts.

m5-t2.introduction: Make social delivery repeatable: choose formats with a purpose, batch the work, keep a small brand kit and schedule with a human review step.

sections.title: Different formats remove different barriers
sections.explanation: Choose a format because it helps the customer make progress, not because the format is fashionable.

items.label: Discover
items.detail: A short visual hook introduces a relevant idea.

items.label: Understand
items.detail: A carousel or guide explains the steps.

items.label: Trust
items.detail: A genuine demonstration or authorised story supplies proof.

items.label: Act
items.detail: A clear offer post or useful link names the next step.

sections.takeaway: One format can serve more than one stage. Judge its message and customer context.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Batch by task, not by last-minute panic
sections.explanation: Separating research, drafting and production reduces switching and makes review easier.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Choose topics, stages, owners and dates.

items.label: Produce
items.detail: Group writing, filming and design tasks.

items.label: Review / schedule
items.detail: Check facts, accessibility, links and timing.

items.label: Listen / learn
items.detail: Reply, record outcomes and feed the next batch.

sections.takeaway: Leave room for timely updates and corrections rather than filling every available slot.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: A small kit creates recognisable work
sections.explanation: A brand kit is a set of reusable decisions, not a rule that every post must look identical.

items.label: Visual rules
items.detail: Use a readable colour palette, type styles and spacing.

items.label: Templates
items.detail: Create a few reusable layouts for real formats.

items.label: Voice
items.detail: Keep tone and wording consistent with the business.

items.label: Quality check
items.detail: Check contrast, captions, permissions and logo use.

sections.takeaway: Consistency should make the content easier to recognise and use, not harder to read.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The brand kit: recognisable without a designer

sections.title: A scheduler is not an approval process
sections.explanation: Tools can queue a post; people must still check whether it is accurate and appropriate when it goes live.

items.label: Prepare
items.detail: Keep approved assets and copy together.

items.label: Validate
items.detail: Check the destination link, preview and accessibility.

items.label: Schedule
items.detail: Use an available approved tool and record the owner.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Confirm publication and respond to the audience.

sections.takeaway: Pause queued content when context changes. Scheduling is not permission to stop paying attention.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: What is still needed after a post is scheduled?
checkpoint.answer: A publication check, context awareness, audience response and outcome logging. The scheduling tool does not replace editorial ownership.

m5-t3.introduction: Treat replies as part of the customer experience. Separate ordinary questions from complaints and sensitive incidents before deciding who responds.

sections.title: The conversation is part of the offer
sections.explanation: A public reply teaches everyone watching what the business is like to deal with.

items.label: Listen
items.detail: Read the actual question and context.

items.label: Respond
items.detail: Answer helpfully without unnecessary defensiveness.

items.label: Resolve
items.detail: Route the real issue to someone who can act.

items.label: Learn
items.detail: Record repeated concerns and improve the offer or content.

sections.takeaway: A reply count is not a service outcome. Check whether the issue was actually resolved.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: A reply matrix reduces improvisation
sections.explanation: Choose the response route by the nature of the message and the risk involved.

items.label: Helpful answer
items.detail: Answer a genuine general question clearly.

items.label: Order support
items.detail: Move account-specific details into an approved private channel.

items.label: Calm acknowledgement
items.detail: Acknowledge concern without repeating private facts.

items.label: Escalate
items.detail: Route safety, legal or serious privacy issues to the named owner.

sections.takeaway: Do not ask for phone numbers, order IDs or other personal details in a public comment.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The four-part complaint reply
sections.explanation: A complaint response should show understanding and a path to action, not a public argument.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.detail: Recognise the experience the person describes.

items.label: Take responsibility
items.detail: Own the investigation without inventing facts.

items.label: Move safely
items.detail: Offer an appropriate private support route.

items.label: Close the loop
items.detail: Name the next step and follow through.

sections.takeaway: Avoid promising a refund, deadline or outcome before the responsible team confirms it.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The anatomy of a public complaint reply

sections.title: Decide the escalation route before a crisis
sections.explanation: Write down who owns serious incidents, who approves communication and what must not be disclosed.

items.label: Triage
items.detail: Identify urgency, potential harm and private information.

items.label: Route
items.detail: Notify the accountable owner through the approved channel.

items.label: Respond safely
items.detail: Use a factual holding response if authorised.

items.label: Record / review
items.detail: Keep the incident trail and update the playbook.

sections.takeaway: Do not leave safety or legal issues to the least experienced person on the account.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. Escalation rules — written before the crisis

sections.title: Rituals create a reason to return
sections.explanation: A small repeatable activity can support a real community when participation is voluntary and useful.

items.label: Weekly questions
items.detail: Offer a predictable time for practical answers.

items.label: Member contributions
items.detail: Invite stories or tips with permission to share.

items.label: Recognition
items.detail: Thank people without exposing personal details.

sections.takeaway: A ritual should serve participants, not pressure them into promotional work.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A customer posts an order number and a complaint. Should the brand repeat those details?
checkpoint.answer: No. Acknowledge calmly, avoid amplifying personal information and move the specific case to an approved private support route. Escalate if the issue is sensitive or urgent.

m5-t4.introduction: Choose creators for fit and evidence, not follower count alone. Make rights, disclosure and measurement part of the brief, then build a responsible UGC loop.

sections.title: Creator size is one dimension, not the verdict
sections.explanation: Different scales can serve different objectives. Reach does not automatically equal relevant influence or useful action.

items.label: Local / niche
items.detail: A smaller relevant audience may support trust and precise community fit.

items.label: Broader specialist
items.detail: A larger topic-focused audience can extend a relevant message.

items.label: Mass reach
items.detail: A large audience needs careful cost, fit and outcome reasoning.

sections.takeaway: Follower-tier labels are rough categories, not a standardised guarantee of reach, price or performance.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The tiers and what each is actually for

sections.title: Evaluate the audience behind the number
sections.explanation: Review recent work, genuine interaction and audience relevance before agreeing to a collaboration.

items.label: Audience match
items.detail: Check geography, need and likely relevance to the offer.

items.label: Content quality
items.detail: Inspect clarity, claims and consistency.

items.label: Interaction quality
items.detail: Read comments; look beyond a raw engagement total.

items.label: Commercial integrity
items.detail: Check disclosure habits, permissions and realistic reporting.

sections.takeaway: Engagement rates only compare fairly when the numerator, denominator and time window match.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The brief protects both sides
sections.explanation: A useful creator brief joins the creative job to commercial and ethical boundaries.

items.label: Creative job
items.detail: Audience, key message, supported claims and CTA.

items.label: Deliverables
items.detail: Formats, dates, review rounds and approval owner.

items.label: Rights / disclosure
items.detail: Usage period, editing rights, paid amplification and clear sponsorship disclosure.

items.label: Measurement
items.detail: Agreed evidence, tagged destinations and reporting dates.

sections.takeaway: Do not assume a fee buys unlimited reuse or permission to run the creator’s content as an ad.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: UGC compounds only with permission
sections.explanation: A repeatable user-generated-content system asks, obtains permission, credits appropriately and measures usefulness.

items.label: Invite
items.detail: Ask for a genuine story without demanding positive claims.

items.label: Obtain permission
items.detail: Agree how and where the content can be reused.

items.label: Curate / publish
items.detail: Preserve meaning and credit as agreed.

items.label: Respond / learn
items.detail: Thank contributors and record helpful outcomes.

sections.takeaway: A public post is not automatically permission for a business to reuse the image in advertising.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Can a brand reuse a public customer photo in a paid ad without asking?
checkpoint.answer: Do not assume so. Obtain the necessary permissions and usage rights, respect personal data and any people depicted, and keep the agreed disclosure and reuse scope clear.

m5-pb3.introduction: Bring the earlier modules into one executable two-week plan. Check coherence between the brief, arithmetic, calendar and measurement before a teammate runs it.

sections.title: One campaign, connected channel roles
sections.explanation: An integrated campaign is not several unrelated posts and ads. Each component should support the same audience and goal.

items.label: Search / content
items.detail: Answer the needs identified by research.

items.label: Paid
items.detail: Use a justified structure, landing page and pre-flight forecast.

items.label: Social / community
items.detail: Operate formats, replies and appropriate creator or UGC work.

items.label: Measurement
items.detail: Define useful outcomes, tags and decision rules.

sections.takeaway: The plan should be executable by another person without guessing at the campaign’s purpose.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The handover pack has a dependency chain
sections.explanation: Put the strategy and numbers before the task list so every action has a reason.

items.label: Brief + funnel
items.detail: State the audience, goal, rates and margin-aware cost guardrail.

items.label: Channel plans
items.detail: Link organic, paid and social components to those assumptions.

items.label: Daily calendar
items.detail: Name assets, owners, dates, destinations and tags.

items.label: Controls + integrity
items.detail: Add measurement, contingencies, reflection and AI disclosure.

sections.takeaway: Use the original submission list to check all required documents; this flow is an organising aid.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: A budget needs an explicit allocation
sections.explanation: This hypothetical ₹10,000 allocation is a practice example of a core, secondary and experimental split, not a required spend.

items.label: Core activity
items.detail: 70% for the best-supported role in this example.

items.label: Secondary activity
items.detail: 20% for a complementary role.

items.label: Experiment
items.detail: 10% for one controlled learning question.

sections.takeaway: The actual plan needs at least three channels including one owned route. Organic-only plans can allocate time and disclose zero media spend; do not pretend effort is free.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

sections.title: Review the arithmetic before the calendar locks
sections.explanation: A peer challenge is useful when it can still change the plan.

items.label: Update the brief
items.detail: Use the evidence learned since Module 1.

items.label: Build the components
items.detail: Complete paid, organic and social operational detail.

items.label: Challenge
items.detail: Ask a partner to find one unsupported number and one missing calendar row.

items.label: Resolve / submit
items.detail: Check the forecast, owners, stop rules and contingencies.

sections.takeaway: A realistic plan states what happens if tracking fails, costs rise or the team misses an asset deadline.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Judge the plan by executability
sections.explanation: The strongest campaign document makes trade-offs, actions and controls visible.

items.label: Strategic coherence
items.detail: Every component traces back to the audience, brief and funnel.

items.label: Operational craft
items.detail: Campaign structure, creative, replies and calendar are usable.

items.label: Measurable control
items.detail: Arithmetic, thresholds and contingencies are explicit.

sections.takeaway: The published rubric remains the assessment authority; the visual summary adds no new grading requirements.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A plan contains three channels but no clear owned route. Is it ready?
checkpoint.answer: No. Check the original coverage requirements, add an appropriate permission-based owned relationship, and make its role, owner and measurement explicit.
